title: US politics, industry divides and the challenge of global AI rules
label: 14 October 2026 · Multilateralism: AI
summary: Witnesses Ian Bremmer and Aalok Mehta set out how the US debate on AI is sharply divided between worried publics, a split tech sector, and an Administration focused on competition with China. Industry wants standards and safety work but cannot unilaterally slow frontier research; the US prefers transactional partnerships that secure supply chains rather than broad global governance. Both witnesses stress the urgent need for international testing, verification and new institutions if we are to manage risks like cyberattacks, job disruption and strategic competition.

chapters.title: How the US debate looks right now
chapters.takeaway: Americans are fearful of AI and US politics, tech firms and the public disagree sharply on how to proceed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want your read on the US debate about AI—what's happening and why it matters to multilateralism.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Surveys show Americans are unusually fearful about AI and losing jobs. That reflects low trust in political and business leaders.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: The political divide is acute: President Trump pushes a hands-off, accelerate approach; many leaders at AI firms call for pauses or stricter safety.

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: Public opinion wants more regulation and accountability. The Administration started deregulatory, but incidents with cyber-capable models have softened that stance.

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: Right now the US relies on industry self-regulation plus existing agencies like the FTC to police deceptive or unsafe practices.

chapters.title: What 'multilateral' means for US policy
chapters.takeaway: The US prefers transactional partnerships to secure advantage and supply chains, not broad global governance.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blackstone
turns.text: How engaged is the US multilateral effort, which department leads, and what's the underlying approach?

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: There are US–China conversations—Trump and Xi met often—but they're mostly talk so far. The US is pushing allies to work with it, not to create joint global rules.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Initiatives like Pax Silica aim to steer investment, compute and supply chains toward US partners. That's hub-and-spoke, not shared global governance.

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: The US approach is transactional: secure supply chains, promote US exports, and keep US firms dominant. That explains resistance to UN-style global oversight.

turns.speaker: Baroness Crawley
turns.text: Is the US–China competition real given the scale of US private investment versus China's?

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: They compete on different things: US spends heavily to push frontier capability; China focuses on diffusion—cheaper models, turnkey solutions, and outreach to other countries.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Also watch for IP theft and Chinese efforts to adopt and spread AI tools. That dims the prospect of cooperative global governance.

chapters.title: Industry's role and limits
chapters.takeaway: Tech firms want standards and safety work, but commercial pressure and a prisoner’s dilemma make unilateral slowdowns unlikely.

turns.speaker: Lord Lamont of Lerwick
turns.text: Is industry pushing for multilateral standards? Can it fill the governance gap?

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: Yes, firms and standards bodies want multilateral standards because it simplifies compliance and addresses public worry; their voluntary commitments often become legal scaffolding.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Companies are building internal safety teams, red-teaming each other's models, and strengthening sandboxes—but they worry that models can 'escape' those sandboxes.

turns.speaker: Lord Ahmad of Wimbledon
turns.text: Industry talks about brakes or kill switches—how would that work globally, especially with China?

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: A US-only pause won't work because of the prisoner’s dilemma: firms fear losing market ground, and any pause must include China to be meaningful—but verification between the US and China is very hard.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Some propose a FINRA-style or a 'technology stability board' to surface and contain threats—an industry-plus-government body modeled on financial regulators.

chapters.title: Politics, jobs and elections
chapters.takeaway: AI will be an electoral issue: Democrats likely to press regulation and safety nets; Republicans favour industry-led growth and competition with China.

turns.speaker: Lord Grocott
turns.text: Will party politics crystalise into clear positions by 2028?

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Yes, but much depends on which candidates emerge. Expect Democrats to press for more oversight; many Republicans, influenced by donors like Elon Musk, will favour a freer hand for industry.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Practical politics already shows bipartisan worries—backlash against data centres, local economic impact, and job anxiety in red and blue areas.

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: By 2028 AI will be a campaign issue. If governments fail to answer public concerns about jobs and accountability, political pressure for regulation will grow.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Even if catastrophic scenarios are low probability, the economic stakes and pace of change mean we must take governance seriously now.

chapters.title: What the UK and others can do
chapters.takeaway: Smaller powers can help by building testing, verification and sovereignty-ready procurement; the UK is well placed to be a trusted evaluator.

turns.speaker: Lord Bruce of Bennachie
turns.text: How should the UK position itself between the US and China?

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: Tactically, the UK should get access to powerful US models for cybersecurity testing and ensure procurement meets data sovereignty needs.

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: Strategically, the AI Security Institute is a major asset: it can benchmark models, act as a trusted third party in any US–China deal, and help verification.

turns.speaker: Lord Alderdice
turns.text: Is there any chance the US will lead a multilateral treaty or new institution?

turns.speaker: Aalok Mehta
turns.text: Under the current Administration, a broad treaty or new UN-style body is unlikely. Expect engagement around standards, export controls, and supply-chain security instead.

turns.speaker: Ian Bremmer
turns.text: Don't assume today's US stance is fixed. Crisis moments often change politics; we should use the time now to design institutions that survive crises and aren't reactive.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. Your bottom line: act fast, build trusted testing and verification, and prepare international mechanisms before the next crisis.
